name: Timucua
sweep_summary: Timucua (timu1245) is in the catalog as EXCLUDED (unit 'in': false, reason 'lexical': stress placement conditioned on morpheme identity, decided on Broadwell 2024 ch. 5 section 5.6 pp. 48-53 at page grade plus Pareja 1614 f8v-9r; the target record's catalog_quote/cite fields are empty but the current catalog unit detail and our earlier reading sections 9-11 carry the decision). The single target item, Granberry 1956 IJAL 22(2):97-105 (doi 10.1086/464353; Chicago landing page 403/paywalled), is OPEN on archive.org as the unrestricted microfilm scan of the whole issue and was already held by the project (page-pinned 2026-08-17); this search of works with stress in the title extracted the article pages, re-read section 2.2 on the p. 102 image, and saved everything under with. Granberry states a nonphonemic, length-conditioned default (initial stress for 1-3 syllables; initial primary plus one secondary on penult or antepenult for longer words; ultima never stressed) plus enclitic-conjunction attraction of primary stress (-tí, -kʷí, -ku ~ hikú; dubitive vs non-dubitive contrast) and penult/antepenult variance of the secondary. classification: REFINES — it supplies the length-only default the catalog knowingly un-adopted, while its own enclitic clause is morpheme-conditioned and does not contradict the 'lexical' exclusion. Two supplementary on-disk sources were re-read for context: Broadwell 2024 section 5.6 (the deciding source; confirms the exclusion: suffix-specific attraction -hecó/-cò/-quì/-ma-tê vs non-attracting -co/-nco, penult before -te/-co/participial -ta with named counterexamples, ergative -ta different, accent marking sporadic and diacritic differences printing artifacts; Granberry not cited in the section) and Pareja 1614 in the Adam & Vinson 1886 edition (open on archive.org; the primary rule: accent on the first vowel for 1-3 vowel words, never on the last for longer, with conjunction-specific exceptions). Nothing remains to acquire: all relevant statements are held by the project at page grade; no item is paywalled-only. none is recorded in the project's existing lit-review files either. Best first-hand statement read: Granberry 1956:102 section 2.2 (does not supersede Broadwell 2024 as the deciding source).

new_statements.quote: 2.2. Nonphonemic stress accent characterizes Timucua utterances. Words of one, two, or three syllables have stress accent on the first syllable, e.g. yúwu (yobo) stone, úkʷu (oquo) flesh, kʷí (quí) and, nípita (nipita) mouth, árukʷi (aruqui) child. Words of more than three syllables generally have primary stress on the first syllable with secondary stress on the penult or antepenult, e.g. átimùku (atimucu) frost, tírakùkula (téracócola) best. [...] Except in the above cases the ultima never receives stress.
new_statements.citation: Granberry, Julian (1956). Timucua I: Prosodics and phonemics of the Mocama dialect. International Journal of American Linguistics 22(2): 97-105. doi:10.1086/464353
new_statements.locator: section 2.2, p. 102 (right column), continued at p. 103 top ('Except in the above cases the ultima never receives stress'); fn. 16 p. 102 defines acute = primary, grave = secondary; verified on the p. 102 page image
new_statements.reading: Granberry's reconstruction (from Pareja's 1614 orthography; no speakers) is a length-only default — initial primary stress for 1-3 syllable words; initial primary plus a single secondary on the penult or antepenult for longer words (átimùku 4σ = 1010, tírakùkula 5σ = 10100), no iteration, ultima never stressed — overlaid with morpheme-conditioned attraction: the enclitic conjunctions -tí, -kʷí, -ku ~ hikú take primary stress (kùyu-kú, hùlata-ma-kʷí), and -ku ~ hikú is stressed only in its dubitive function (àku-kú vs áku-ku); he also records that the secondary 'varies between the penult and antepenult' (p. 103). The catalog's exclusion code 'lexical' (placement conditioned on morpheme identity, Broadwell 2024:48-53) is not contradicted by this page: Granberry's own enclitic clause is morpheme-conditioned, and Broadwell's page-grade corpus reading (penult before -te/-co/-ta, -hecó/-cò/-quì attract, -co/-nco do not, Pareja's own examples breaking initial stress, accent marking sporadic outside ~20 folia) is the more authoritative modern account and remains the deciding source. Granberry 1956 stays the best first-hand statement of the un-adopted length-only default.

audit.reasoning: Coding: 'excluded' (lexical / morpheme-conditioned placement; StressTyp2's 1L+i2@1L fixed code rejected). Every source opened agrees the pattern is not a length-only rule: Pareja 1614 ff.8v-9v (downloaded now, page grade) gives initial accent for 1-3-vowel words and 'never final' for longer ones but immediately lists his own non-initial examples (nahíabotela, mitánicala) and a closed set of enclitics/suffixes that take final accent (-hecó, -có, -quí, -maté) versus homophonous -co/-qui that do not; Granberry 1956:102 (held image) reconstructs initial primary + penult/antepenult secondary with enclitics taking primary stress; Broadwell 2024:48-53 (held PDF), the 476-pp text-based reference grammar, declines Granberry's reconstruction, documents suffix-conditioned penult stress in the corpus and calls the analysis uncertain with penult as the likely default. Initial-vs-penult default is unresolved be

sources.note: A length-conditioned default reconstructed from Pareja's 1614 orthography (no speakers): primary stress on the first syllable in 1-3 syllable words; in longer words initial primary plus ONE secondary on the penult or antepenult (átimùku 4σ: secondary on penult; tírakùkula 5σ: secondary on antepenult); no iterative secondaries. sources.quote: The data are not completely consistent, but the main pattern is that the affix -hecó 'if' (also written -hêco) attracts stress, as do the affixes -cò and -quì 'and', and the sequence of affixes -ma-tê 'and the'. [...] The main pattern here is that contracted adjectives, plus the -co 'alternative' and -nco 'indefinite' suffixes do not attract word stress. [...] The use of accent marks in the text corpus only partially matches Pareja's description. Accent marking is sporadic in most texts, with the exception of about the first twenty folia in Pareja (1627a).
sources.locator: section 5.6.1 pp. 48-50 (Pareja's description, table 14 'Suffixes that attract stress'); 5.6.2 pp. 50-53 (accent marking in the corpus; tables 15-17: penult before -te, -co, -ta participial)
sources.note: Quotes Pareja 1614 f8v-9r (accent on the first vowel for words of 1-3 vowels, never on the last vowel for longer words), then shows Pareja's own examples break it (nahìabotela / nahìabotamala: stress on σ2; mìla 'I am going' vs mitânicala 'we are going': stress shifts with the plural). Stress attraction is morpheme-specific: -hecó, -cò, -quì, -ma-tê attract; -co 'alternative', -nco 'indefinite' and contracted adjectives do not. Corpus accents (mostly the first ~20 folia of Pareja 1627a) show penult stress before -te 'contrastive' (table 15, with antepenult counterexamples holatàmate, qiemìmat…

sources.quote: Totas las diciones que tuuieren una ó dos, ó tres vocales, se a de poner el accento en la primera vocal, y si mas tuuiere se advierta que nunca se a de poner en la ultima vocal [...] Sacanse estas diciones, las quales se hallarán en todos los verbos, y en algunos nombres que se pone el acento en la primera ó ultima vocal [...] Pero a se de advertir, que quando no es conjuncion el qui, ni es interrogante el co, no se a de poner el accento en la ultima
sources.locator: 1886 ed. p. 5 (marginal 'F. 8, v°') to p. 6; 'Del Accento y Pronunciacion'
sources.note: Translation: 'All words that have one, two or three vowels must have the accent placed on the first vowel, and if they have more, be advised that it is never to be placed on the last vowel [..] Excepted are these words, which are found in all the verbs, and in some nouns, where the accent is placed on the first or last vowel [..] But note that when qui is not a conjunction, nor co interrogative, the accent is not to be placed on the last [vowel]'.
